title: 1.4 Sports Data Sources and R Packages
1.4 Sports Data Sources and R Packages
1.2 Scraping HTML Data from Websites
text:
1 Learning objectives
After completing this tutorial, you should be able to:

describe the roles of HTML elements, attributes, and text;
select elements with CSS selectors and XPath;
extract text, attributes, links, and tables with rvest;
identify a table by its schema instead of its page position;
validate a scraped result before analysis; and
explain the legal, ethical, and technical limits of web scraping.



2 When scraping is appropriate
HTML scraping extracts information from a page designed primarily for people. Before scraping, ask whether the same information is available through an official API, a downloadable file, or a maintained data repository. Those alternatives usually have a more stable structure.
A responsible workflow includes the following checks:

Review the site’s terms of use, robots.txt, and attribution requirements.
Request only the pages needed for the analysis.
Avoid rapid or repeated requests; cache a permitted local copy.
Identify the data provider and retrieval date.
Do not attempt to bypass authentication, access restrictions, or technical controls.







Warning



A page being visible in a browser does not automatically grant permission to collect, redistribute, or commercialize its contents.




3 How HTML represents a page
HTML uses nested elements. An element normally has an opening tag, content, and a closing tag.
<article class="game-card" data-game-id="G01">
  <h2>Buffalo 21, Miami 14</h2>
  <a class="box-score" href="/games/G01">Box score</a>
</article>
In this example:

article, h2, and a are element names;
class, data-game-id, and href are attributes; and
Buffalo 21, Miami 14 is text.



4 Read a page
read_html() can read either a local HTML file or a permitted web address. We begin with the local teaching page included in this project so that the example remains reproducible.

page <- read_html("data/sample-standings.html")
page

{html_document}
<html lang="en">
[1] <head>\n<meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=UTF-8 ...
[2] <body>\n  <main><h1>Sample Football Results</h1>\n    <p class="updated"> ...


Use html_element() when one match is expected and html_elements() when several matches are expected.

page %>%
  html_element("h1") %>%
  html_text2()

[1] "Sample Football Results"

page %>%
  html_elements("h2") %>%
  html_text2()

[1] "Buffalo 21, Miami 14"       "Dallas 20, Philadelphia 27"




5 CSS selectors
A CSS selector describes the elements to find.



Selector
Meaning




h2
Every <h2> element


.game-card
Elements whose class includes game-card


#standings
The element whose id is standings


[data-game-id]
Elements containing the named attribute


.game-card h2
<h2> elements inside a game card


a.box-score
<a> elements with class box-score



Browser developer tools can help identify candidate selectors. Prefer selectors based on meaningful IDs, classes, and attributes rather than long paths tied to the visual layout.

game_cards <- page %>%
  html_elements(".game-card")

length(game_cards)

[1] 2




6 Extract structured values
html_text2() extracts visible-style text with normalized spacing. html_attr() extracts an attribute.

featured_games <- tibble(
  game_id = game_cards %>%
    html_attr("data-game-id"),
  result = game_cards %>%
    html_element("h2") %>%
    html_text2(),
  status = game_cards %>%
    html_element(".status") %>%
    html_text2(),
  box_score_path = game_cards %>%
    html_element("a.box-score") %>%
    html_attr("href")
)

featured_games

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  game_id result                     status box_score_path
  <chr>   <chr>                      <chr>  <chr>         
1 G01     Buffalo 21, Miami 14       Final  /games/G01    
2 G02     Dallas 20, Philadelphia 27 Final  /games/G02    


Always compare the number of extracted values with the number of source elements. If an expected child is absent, html_element() returns a missing element and the extracted value becomes NA, which helps keep rows aligned.


7 Extract tables
html_table() converts an HTML table into a tibble. A page may contain standings, navigation tables, advertisements, and unrelated statistics, so selecting the first or third table is fragile.

page_tables <- page %>%
  html_elements("table") %>%
  html_table(trim = TRUE)

length(page_tables)

[1] 2

lapply(page_tables, names)

[[1]]
[1] "Partner" "Message"

[[2]]
[1] "Team"               "W"                  "L"                 
[4] "Point differential"


The teaching page deliberately places an advertisement table before the standings table. Select the desired table by its required columns.

required_columns <- c("Team", "W", "L", "Point differential")

is_standings_table <- vapply(
  page_tables,
  function(table) all(required_columns %in% names(table)),
  logical(1)
)

is_standings_table

[1] FALSE  TRUE


Now extract and clean the matching table.

standings <- page_tables[[which(is_standings_table)]] %>%
  rename(
    wins = W,
    losses = L,
    point_differential = `Point differential`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    wins = as.integer(wins),
    losses = as.integer(losses),
    point_differential = parse_number(as.character(point_differential))
  )

standings

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  Team          wins losses point_differential
  <chr>        <int>  <int>              <dbl>
1 Baltimore       13      4                203
2 Buffalo         11      6                140
3 Dallas          12      5                194
4 Philadelphia    11      6                  5


parse_number() removes symbols such as a leading plus sign and returns a numeric value. Inspect the output before relying on automatic conversion.


8 XPath
XPath is another language for navigating an HTML tree. CSS selectors are usually easier for straightforward page scraping, while XPath is useful for relationships that are difficult to express with CSS.
The following XPath selects the first table whose header cells include the text Point differential:

standings_with_xpath <- page %>%
  html_element(xpath = "//table[.//th[contains(., 'Point differential')]]") %>%
  html_table(trim = TRUE)

standings_with_xpath

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  Team             W     L `Point differential`
  <chr>        <int> <int>                <int>
1 Baltimore       13     4                  203
2 Buffalo         11     6                  140
3 Dallas          12     5                  194
4 Philadelphia    11     6                    5


Common XPath patterns include:







XPath
Meaning




//table
Every table anywhere in the document


//article[@data-game-id]
Articles containing a data-game-id attribute


//a/@href
Every link destination attribute


//comment()
HTML comment nodes





9 Write a reusable scraper
A function should express its assumptions and stop with a useful message when the page no longer matches them.

read_standings_table <- function(source) {
  tables <- read_html(source) %>%
    html_elements("table") %>%
    html_table(trim = TRUE)

  required <- c("Team", "W", "L", "Point differential")
  keep <- vapply(
    tables,
    function(table) all(required %in% names(table)),
    logical(1)
  )

  if (sum(keep) != 1) {
    stop(
      "Expected exactly one standings table; found ",
      sum(keep),
      "."
    )
  }

  tables[[which(keep)]] %>%
    rename(
      wins = W,
      losses = L,
      point_differential = `Point differential`
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      wins = as.integer(wins),
      losses = as.integer(losses),
      point_differential = parse_number(as.character(point_differential))
    )
}

standings_checked <- read_standings_table(
  "data/sample-standings.html"
)

standings_checked

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  Team          wins losses point_differential
  <chr>        <int>  <int>              <dbl>
1 Baltimore       13      4                203
2 Buffalo         11      6                140
3 Dallas          12      5                194
4 Philadelphia    11      6                  5




10 Validate the result
A request can succeed while returning the wrong content. Check assumptions that matter to the analysis.

stopifnot(
  nrow(standings_checked) == 4,
  !anyDuplicated(standings_checked$Team),
  all(standings_checked$wins >= 0),
  all(standings_checked$losses >= 0),
  all(standings_checked$wins + standings_checked$losses == 17)
)

Useful checks include expected columns, unique identifiers, plausible ranges, row counts, missingness, and comparisons with a known value on the source page.


11 Move from a local page to a website
Once the parser works on a saved example, the same functions can read a permitted URL.

standings_url <- paste0(
  "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/",
  "2018_Major_League_Baseball_season"
)

live_page <- read_html(standings_url)

live_page %>%
  html_element(".MLBStandingsTable") %>%
  html_table() %>%
  bind_rows()

Do not assume that selectors from the teaching page apply to another website. Inspect the new page, identify its schema, and write new validation rules.


12 Why scrapers fail
A scraper may stop working because:

an ID, class, heading, or table schema changed;
the server returned a consent page, rate-limit response, or access-denied page;
JavaScript creates the content after the initial HTML loads;
a table is stored inside an HTML comment;
repeated headers or merged cells change the parsed rows; or
the visible page is a presentation layer over an undocumented API.

For JavaScript-generated pages, rvest::read_html_live() can control a browser-backed session. This approach has more dependencies and should not be used to bypass access controls. If the page retrieves data from a documented API, use that API instead.


13 Practice

Extract the page title and the update date from the local teaching page.
Extract the text and href value from every box-score link.
Select the standings table directly with the CSS selector #standings.
Modify read_standings_table() so it also calculates winning percentage.
Explain why page_tables[[2]] is less reliable than a schema check.







TipShow answers






# 1. Page title and update date
page_title <- page %>%
  html_element("title") %>%
  html_text2()

update_date <- page %>%
  html_element(".updated") %>%
  html_text2()

page_title
update_date

# 2. Box-score link text and destination
box_score_links <- page %>%
  html_elements("a.box-score")

tibble(
  text = box_score_links %>% html_text2(),
  href = box_score_links %>% html_attr("href")
)

# 3. Select the table directly by ID
page %>%
  html_element("#standings") %>%
  html_table(trim = TRUE)

# 4. Add winning percentage
read_standings_with_percentage <- function(source) {
  read_standings_table(source) %>%
    mutate(winning_percentage = wins / (wins + losses))
}

5. A position can change when an unrelated table is inserted or removed. A schema check states which variables are required and fails clearly when the expected structure is absent.





14 Key takeaways

Inspect the page structure before writing extraction code.
Prefer short, meaningful selectors tied to content rather than visual position.
Use html_elements() for repeated records and html_element() for one child per record.
Select tables by required fields, not by list position.
Validate every scraped result and expect the page structure to change.
Follow access rules and prefer an API or maintained download when available.



15 References

rvest documentation
CSS selector reference
html_table() documentation

title: R Foundations and Sports Data Acquisition
text:
1 Overview
This lecture covers the basics of R programming language for sports analytics. It begins with R objects, matrix calculations, and tidy data manipulation; then moves from HTML pages to JSON APIs; and finishes by comparing R packages for sports data.


2 Tutorial map








Tutorial
Main question
Core skills




1.1
How does R represent and transform data?
Vectors, lists, matrices, data frames, matrix algebra, and dplyr


1.2
How can data be extracted from an HTML page responsibly?
HTML structure, CSS selectors, XPath, tables, and validation


1.3
How do programs exchange structured web data?
JSON, HTTP requests, APIs, nested records, and error handling


1.4
Which sports-data source should an analyst use?
Popular R packages for sports analytics





3 Required packages
Install packages once in the R console. Do not place installation commands in code that runs every time a tutorial is rendered.

install.packages(c(
  "dplyr",
  "httr2",
  "jsonlite",
  "readr",
  "rvest"
))

The sports-specific packages in Tutorial 1.4 are optional. Install only the packages needed for the sport and research question.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
3.1 Atomic vectors
An atomic vector contains values of one basic type. Important types include logical, integer, double, character, and date-time values.

completed_passes <- c(18L, 22L, 15L)
completion_rates <- c(0.64, 0.71, 0.58)
teams <- c("BUF", "KC", "PHI")
made_playoffs <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

typeof(completed_passes)

[1] "integer"

length(teams)

[1] 3


When incompatible types are combined, R converts them to a common type. This behavior is called coercion.

c(1, TRUE, "BUF")

[1] "1"    "TRUE" "BUF" 


Missing values are represented by NA. Many summary functions require an explicit decision about whether to remove them.

snap_counts <- c(62, 58, NA, 71)

mean(snap_counts)

[1] NA

mean(snap_counts, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 63.66667

is.na(snap_counts)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
3.2 Factors
A factor stores categorical values and their allowed levels. Set the level order deliberately when it carries meaning.

game_phase <- factor(
  c("regular season", "postseason", "regular season"),
  levels = c("preseason", "regular season", "postseason")
)

game_phase

[1] regular season postseason     regular season
Levels: preseason regular season postseason

levels(game_phase)

[1] "preseason"      "regular season" "postseason"

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
3.3 Lists
A list can contain objects of different types and sizes. Lists are common in JSON responses and model output.

player <- list(
  name = "Example Quarterback",
  position = "QB",
  weekly_yards = c(245, 310, 278),
  active = TRUE
)

player$position

[1] "QB"

player[["weekly_yards"]]

[1] 245 310 278

player["weekly_yards"]

$weekly_yards
[1] 245 310 278


[[ extracts the object stored in one list element. [ returns a smaller list. $ extracts a named element and is convenient for interactive work.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
3.4 Matrices and arrays
A matrix is a two-dimensional atomic vector. Every cell therefore has the same type.

player_stats <- matrix(
  c(245, 2, 310, 3, 278, 1),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    week = paste0("Week ", 1:3),
    statistic = c("passing_yards", "touchdowns")
  )
)

player_stats

        statistic
week     passing_yards touchdowns
  Week 1           245          2
  Week 2           310          3
  Week 3           278          1

player_stats[2, "passing_yards"]

[1] 310

player_stats[, "touchdowns"]

Week 1 Week 2 Week 3 
     2      3      1 


An array generalizes a matrix to more than two dimensions.

tracking_grid <- array(
  1:24,
  dim = c(x_position = 4, y_position = 3, frame = 2)
)

dim(tracking_grid)

x_position y_position      frame 
         4          3          2 

tracking_grid[, , 1]

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    5    9
[2,]    2    6   10
[3,]    3    7   11
[4,]    4    8   12

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
3.5 Data frames and tibbles
A data frame is rectangular: each row is an observation and each column is a variable. Columns may have different types, but every column must have the same number of rows. A tibble is a modern data frame with more readable printing and stricter behavior.

games <- tibble(
  game_id = paste0("G", 1:8),
  home_team = c("BUF", "KC", "PHI", "SF", "BUF", "KC", "PHI", "SF"),
  away_team = c("MIA", "CIN", "DAL", "SEA", "NYJ", "LV", "NYG", "LAR"),
  home_score = c(31, 24, 21, 27, 17, 30, 28, 20),
  away_score = c(24, 27, 17, 20, 20, 13, 10, 23),
  home_turnovers = c(1, 2, 0, 1, 3, 0, 1, 2),
  away_turnovers = c(2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1)
)

games

# A tibble: 8 × 7
  game_id home_team away_team home_score away_score home_turnovers
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>          <dbl>
1 G1      BUF       MIA               31         24              1
2 G2      KC        CIN               24         27              2
3 G3      PHI       DAL               21         17              0
4 G4      SF        SEA               27         20              1
5 G5      BUF       NYJ               17         20              3
6 G6      KC        LV                30         13              0
7 G7      PHI       NYG               28         10              1
8 G8      SF        LAR               20         23              2
# ℹ 1 more variable: away_turnovers <dbl>

glimpse(games)

Rows: 8
Columns: 7
$ game_id        <chr> "G1", "G2", "G3", "G4", "G5", "G6", "G7", "G8"
$ home_team      <chr> "BUF", "KC", "PHI", "SF", "BUF", "KC", "PHI", "SF"
$ away_team      <chr> "MIA", "CIN", "DAL", "SEA", "NYJ", "LV", "NYG", "LAR"
$ home_score     <dbl> 31, 24, 21, 27, 17, 30, 28, 20
$ away_score     <dbl> 24, 27, 17, 20, 20, 13, 10, 23
$ home_turnovers <dbl> 1, 2, 0, 1, 3, 0, 1, 2

These are small teaching data created for this tutorial, not an official historical data set.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
4.1 Transpose, identity, and determinant
The transpose A𝖳A^\mathsf{T} exchanges rows and columns. An identity matrix has ones on its diagonal and behaves like the number 1 in matrix multiplication.

t(A)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    1
[2,]    1    3

diag(2)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    0
[2,]    0    1

det(A)

[1] 5


For this matrix,
det⁡(A)=(2)(3)−(1)(1)=5.
\det(A)=(2)(3)-(1)(1)=5.

Because the determinant is not zero, AA is invertible.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
4.2 Element-wise and matrix multiplication
A * A multiplies corresponding cells. A %*% A performs matrix multiplication.

A * A

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    4    1
[2,]    1    9

A %*% A

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    5    5
[2,]    5   10


For matrices Am×nA_{m\times n} and Bn×pB_{n\times p}, the product ABAB has dimension m×pm\times p, and
(AB)ij=∑k=1naikbkj.
(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}b_{kj}.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
4.3 Inverse and a linear system
The inverse A−1A^{-1} satisfies AA−1=IAA^{-1}=I.

A_inverse <- solve(A)
A_inverse

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  0.6 -0.2
[2,] -0.2  0.4

round(A %*% A_inverse, digits = 10)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    0
[2,]    0    1


For a 2×22\times2 matrix,
[abcd]−1=1ad−bc[d−b−ca].
\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}^{-1}
=\frac{1}{ad-bc}
\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}.

Therefore,
A−1=15[3−1−12].
A^{-1}=\frac{1}{5}
\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}.

Solving Ax=bAx=b gives x=A−1bx=A^{-1}b.

x <- solve(A, b)
x

[1] 1.6 1.8

A %*% x

     [,1]
[1,]    5
[2,]    7


In numerical work, prefer solve(A, b) to calculating solve(A) %*% b. It is usually faster and more stable. An inverse does not exist for a singular matrix, and a nearly singular matrix can produce unstable results.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
4.4 Connection to linear regression
For the linear model
y=Xβ+ε,
y=X\beta+\varepsilon,

the ordinary least-squares estimate is
β̂=(X𝖳X)−1X𝖳y.
\widehat{\beta}=(X^\mathsf{T}X)^{-1}X^\mathsf{T}y.

The first column of XX contains ones for the intercept. The second contains an illustrative turnover margin.

turnover_margin <- c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
points_scored <- c(17, 20, 24, 27, 31)

X <- cbind(intercept = 1, turnover_margin = turnover_margin)
y <- points_scored

beta_hat <- solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y)
beta_hat

                [,1]
intercept       23.8
turnover_margin  3.5

coef(lm(points_scored ~ turnover_margin))

    (Intercept) turnover_margin 
           23.8             3.5 


The two calculations agree. In practice, lm() uses a numerically safer matrix decomposition rather than forming the inverse directly.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
5.1 Filter and arrange

game_results %>%
  filter(abs(home_margin) <= 7) %>%
  arrange(abs(home_margin), game_id)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  game_id home_team away_team home_score away_score home_margin home_win
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl> <lgl>   
1 G2      KC        CIN               24         27          -3 FALSE   
2 G5      BUF       NYJ               17         20          -3 FALSE   
3 G8      SF        LAR               20         23          -3 FALSE   
4 G3      PHI       DAL               21         17           4 TRUE    
5 G1      BUF       MIA               31         24           7 TRUE    
6 G4      SF        SEA               27         20           7 TRUE    
# ℹ 1 more variable: turnover_margin <dbl>

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
5.2 Group and summarize

game_results %>%
  group_by(home_team) %>%
  summarize(
    games = n(),
    wins = sum(home_win),
    average_margin = mean(home_margin),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(average_margin))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  home_team games  wins average_margin
  <chr>     <int> <int>          <dbl>
1 PHI           2     2             11
2 KC            2     1              7
3 BUF           2     1              2
4 SF            2     1              2


The .groups = "drop" argument returns an ungrouped result and prevents later operations from unexpectedly retaining the grouping.

title: 1.1 R Foundations and Data Manipulation
text:
5.3 Join related tables
A join connects tables through a key. Here, home_team in the game table corresponds to team in a lookup table.

team_lookup <- tribble(
  ~team, ~conference,
  "BUF", "AFC",
  "KC", "AFC",
  "PHI", "NFC",
  "SF", "NFC"
)

game_results %>%
  left_join(team_lookup, by = c("home_team" = "team")) %>%
  select(game_id, home_team, conference, home_margin)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  game_id home_team conference home_margin
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>            <dbl>
1 G1      BUF       AFC                  7
2 G2      KC        AFC                 -3
3 G3      PHI       NFC                  4
4 G4      SF        NFC                  7
5 G5      BUF       AFC                 -3
6 G6      KC        AFC                 17
7 G7      PHI       NFC                 18
8 G8      SF        NFC                 -3


Before a join, verify that the key is unique on the side expected to contribute one match. Duplicate keys can multiply rows.

title: 1.3 Working with JSON and APIs
1.3 Working with JSON and APIs
text:
5.1 Work with a nested array
Each game also contains an array named drives. After parsing, this becomes a list-column: each row stores a small data frame of drive events.

games$drives[[1]]

  team points
1  ARI      7
2  BUF      3
3  BUF      7


To create one drive table, preserve the parent game_id while combining the nested records.

drive_events <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(games)), function(i) {
  as_tibble(games$drives[[i]]) %>%
    mutate(game_id = games$game_id[[i]], .before = 1)
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

drive_events

# A tibble: 9 × 3
  game_id         team  points
  <chr>           <chr>  <int>
1 2024_01_ARI_BUF ARI        7
2 2024_01_ARI_BUF BUF        3
3 2024_01_ARI_BUF BUF        7
4 2024_01_PIT_ATL ATL        7
5 2024_01_PIT_ATL PIT        3
6 2024_01_PIT_ATL PIT        3
7 2024_01_TEN_CHI TEN        7
8 2024_01_TEN_CHI CHI        3
9 2024_01_TEN_CHI CHI        7


The teaching snapshot includes only a few drives from each game. Their points therefore do not equal the final game scores.

drive_events %>%
  group_by(game_id, team) %>%
  summarize(
    recorded_drives = n(),
    recorded_points = sum(points),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  game_id         team  recorded_drives recorded_points
  <chr>           <chr>           <int>           <int>
1 2024_01_ARI_BUF ARI                 1               7
2 2024_01_ARI_BUF BUF                 2              10
3 2024_01_PIT_ATL ATL                 1               7
4 2024_01_PIT_ATL PIT                 2               6
5 2024_01_TEN_CHI CHI                 2              10
6 2024_01_TEN_CHI TEN                 1               7
